about: CHAIN cnut_1016 (Design/content/CHAINS.md; page Design/content/chains/cnut_1016.md; words Data/writing/chain_cnut_1016.json). Cnut's peace, 1017 to 1037: the tribute of 1018 and the fleet paid off, English irons carried to strike the king's pennies among the Danes, the tolls a shipman meets between the Thames and the Rhine (the monks' haven at the Wantsum mouth, the archbishop's bank at Cologne, the count's water at Flardinga), the Holy River, the king's journey to Rome and his letter of 1027, and what a dead king's writing is worth in 1035. Thirteen cards, three endings (the king's peace as it was; the Rhine named in the letter, which is history changed; the emperor's man, who sold his tally), and a reckoning after the king's death. Flags: ch_cnut_1016_<n> for the steps, ch_cnut_1016_end_<name> for the endings, changed_cnut_letter_rhine, and the spine's en_paid_share, en_followed_silver, en_cnut_peace. Scheduled cards also carry a weight, so a missed day is not a lost story.

cards.note: Step 1, the start (drawn at Lundenwic, Hamwic, Sarre, Dofras or Gipeswic in 1017 and 1018). The tribute is gathered and the fleet waits for its pay. Sources: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1018 (72,000 pounds over all England and 10,500 from the townsmen of London; the army went partly to Denmark and forty ships were left with the king; Danes and English agreed at Oxford to Edgar's law), our rendering; chronicle_793.json 1018-heregeld; dossiers/lundenwic.md. That a stranger's keel was asked for a share is ours (?). Sets ch_cnut_1016_1; the spine's en_paid_share or en_followed_silver.
cards.when: moored and (port.id = lundenwic or port.id = hamwic or port.id = sarre or port.id = dofras or port.id = gipeswic) and year >= 1017 and year <= 1018 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_1

reeve.note: the port-reeve's man with the tally; invented, unnamed

warrior.note: a shipman of the king's fleet waiting to be paid off; invented, unnamed

cards.title: The weighing
cards.intention: The tribute is being gathered over all England, and the town's share is weighed out on a bench by the water. The reeve's man goes from door to door and from keel to keel. The fleet lies in the river and waits.

options.label: Lay down sixty pennies toward the town's share
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s01.out_pay (a stranger's name on the town's tally; step 2 remembers it)

options.label: Sell drink and cloth to the men who are waiting for their pay
options.check: hold.ale > 0 or hold.mead > 0 or hold.rhenish_wine > 0 or hold.frankish_wine > 0 or hold.wool_cloth > 0
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s01.out_sell (30 d of earnest and a true price word: drink is dear here for forty days)

options.label: Say you are a stranger here, and watch the weighing
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s01.out_watch (costs nothing; a riddle on money from the man at the scales)

cards.note: Step 2, and a second start (drawn at Lundenwic, April to September, 1019 to 1023; it does not ask for step 1). A London moneyer is sent with the king's irons to strike pennies among the Danes. Sources: Cnut king in Denmark from 1018 or 1019 and his Danish coinage of about 1020 (realms/denmark.md; economy/silver_coin.md: 'a row of' Danish mints); pennies with Ripa's name from Cnut (dossiers/ripa.md [VSM]); English moneyers' names on Cnut's Danish pennies, chiefly at Lund (later_ports/scandinavia.md) (?). That one of them sailed for Ripa in a merchant's keel is ours. Leofstan is invented (Leof- + -stan). Sets ch_cnut_1016_2; _carried, _moneyer_friend; schedules step 3.
cards.when: moored and port.id = lundenwic and year >= 1019 and year <= 1023 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_2

moneyer.note: Leofstan, a moneyer of Lunden; invented

kings_man.note: a housecarl of the forty ships; invented, unnamed

cards.title: Irons for Denmark
cards.intention: The fleet has gone home and forty ships lie below the bridge. A moneyer of the town stands on the hythe with a locked chest and a boy. The king wants English pennies struck among the Danes, and the irons to strike them are in the chest.

options.label: Carry him and his chest to Ripa for forty pennies
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s02.out_fare

options.label: Carry him for nothing but his good word at the king's mint
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s02.out_word (costs a place in the boat; he changes your coin without his cut in step 3)

options.label: You are not bound for Jutland: ask what the king wants with English irons
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s02.out_hear (costs nothing; he sails with another and the story goes on at Ripa)

memory.fare: carried the moneyer for a fare
memory.word: carried the moneyer for his word

cards.note: Step 3, a turn (Ripa; scheduled nine days after step 2 if he was carried, else drawn there to 1026). The king's pennies are struck at Ripa and the bishop takes his part. Sources: a mint at Ripa by name only from Cnut, 1018 to 1035 (dossiers/ripa.md [VSM]); Odinkar the younger, bishop of Ripa about 1000 to 1043 (Adam of Bremen II (?)); the bishop's half of the king's income from Ripa is ascribed to Cnut, with no charter (dossiers/ripa.md) (?); a moneyer's cut for changing foreign coin from Cnut's time (realms/denmark.md); Denmark goes over to coin by count only in the 1040s to 1060s (economy/silver_coin.md) (?), so the Danes here still weigh. Sets ch_cnut_1016_3; _wine_order.
cards.when: moored and port.id = ripa and flag.ch_cnut_1016_2 and year <= 1026 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_3

moneyer.note: Leofstan, now the king's moneyer at Ripa; invented

clerk.note: a clerk of Bishop Odinkar the younger (historical, bishop about 1000 to 1043); the clerk invented, unnamed

cards.title: One penny on both shores
cards.intention: At Ripa a hearth burns in a shed beside the bishop's church and a hammer rings on iron. The pennies come off the block with the king's head on one face and Ripa's name on the other. The same penny now buys ale on the Thames and on this river.

options.label: Take the bishop's order: six casks of Rhine wine before next summer
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s03.out_wine (the turn: six casks at half as much again, about 180 d over the market; it sends her to the Rhine)

options.label: Change your silver for the king's pennies at his table
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s03.out_change (coin that passes by count here: half the toll on her sales at Ripa for ninety days)

options.label: Ask the moneyer what the Danes make of it
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s03.out_ask (costs nothing; the riddle of the scales)

memory.change: changed silver at the king's table

cards.note: Step 4 (drawn at Sarre, 1023 to 1030, once the story has begun). A toll with a writing behind it: the king gives Christ Church the haven of Sandwich and its tolls on both shores, 'as far inland as a small axe can be thrown from a ship afloat at high tide'. Sources: Sawyer 959, dated 1023, the text as it stands held a later forgery (lore/law_tolls.md; dossiers/sarre.md) (?): the grant itself is generally allowed, the wording doubted. Sandwich has no row in ports_793.json: Sarre, the Wantsum port, stands for it. The monk and the ferryman are invented. Sets ch_cnut_1016_4; _read_writ (step 8 reads it).
cards.when: moored and port.id = sarre and year >= 1023 and year <= 1030 and flag.ch_cnut_1016_2 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_4

monk.note: Christ Church's monk at the haven; invented, unnamed

cards.title: As far as an axe is thrown
cards.intention: The king has given the haven at the Wantsum mouth and its tolls to Christ Church, on both shores. At high water a monk stands in a boat and a ship's boy throws a small axe at the land. Where it falls, the monks' right ends.

options.label: Pay the monks' toll and ask to see the writing
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s04.out_read (the toll as ever, and a little Latin: she now knows a toll with a writing from one without)

options.label: Ask to throw the axe yourself
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s04.out_throw_success or .out_throw_failure (costs pride at the worst)

options.label: Ask the ferryman what he paid before the monks came
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s04.out_ask (costs nothing)

cards.note: Step 5 (drawn at Colonia, 1020 to 1026, once the story has begun). English and Danish pilgrims and two London merchants are tolled as merchants at Cologne, the third time since the river mouth. Sources: the complaint Cnut carried to Rome, 'so many barriers on the way' and 'unjust tolls' on merchants and on those who go to pray (his letter of 1027, William of Malmesbury, Gesta regum II.183; John of Worcester under 1031; lore/law_tolls.md section 10); the old quarrel over merchants who travel as pilgrims (Charles to Offa, 796); Pilgrim, archbishop of Cologne 1021 to 1036. That the letter's tolls were met on the Rhine at Cologne is ours (?): the letter names the road to Rome and King Rudolf's barriers in the mountains. Toke is invented (Danish Toki). Sets ch_cnut_1016_5 and _tally_rhine on every road; _paid_pilgrims.
cards.when: moored and port.id = colonia and year >= 1020 and year <= 1026 and flag.ch_cnut_1016_2 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_5

tollman.note: the archbishop's toll man at the bank; invented, unnamed

pilgrim.note: Toke, a farmer of Jutland bound for Rome; invented

merchant.note: a cloth merchant of Lunden; invented, unnamed

cards.title: The third toll
cards.intention: On the toll bank below the wall of Cologne eleven people sit on their bundles: English and Danes bound for Rome, and two men of Lunden with cloth. The toll man has taken toll from all of them as merchants. It is the third time since the river mouth.

options.label: Pay the pilgrims' toll yourself: forty-five pennies
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s05.out_pay (Toke remembers the boat: step 9 and the endings read it)

options.label: Speak for them: the cloth is their bread, not their trade
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s05.out_speak_success or .out_speak_failure (failure costs ten pennies 'for the showing'; the count is cut on the stick either way)

options.label: Say nothing: count what he takes and cut it on a stick
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s05.out_count (costs nothing)

memory.speak.failure: argued at the toll bank and lost
memory.count: counted the toll on a stick

cards.note: Step 6 (drawn at Traiectum, Noviomagus or Daventre, 1019 to 1026, once the story has begun). The count's toll at the river mouth. Sources: Alpert of Metz, De diversitate temporum II.20-21: the merchants of Tiel complained to the emperor that Count Dirk's men at Flardinga robbed them, and that they could no longer sail to Britain nor the Britons to them; the emperor's army under Duke Godfrey and Bishop Adalbold of Utrecht was beaten in the marsh on 29 July 1018 and the count kept his water (chronicle_793.json 1018-07-29-vlaardingen, 1020-tiel-merchants). Tiel has no row in ports_793.json: the Tiel men are met in the bishop's and the emperor's towns upriver. The Tiel merchant is invented, unnamed. Sets ch_cnut_1016_6; _tally_merwede.
cards.when: moored and (port.id = traiectum or port.id = noviomagus or port.id = daventre) and year >= 1019 and year <= 1026 and flag.ch_cnut_1016_2 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_6

merchant.note: a merchant of Tiel, one of those who swear and drink together; invented, unnamed

cards.title: The count's water
cards.intention: Since the count beat the emperor's army in the marsh at Flardinga, his men sit at the river mouth and take what they please from every keel bound for England. The merchants of Tiel have sent to the emperor twice. They are loading in one company, and there is room in it.

options.label: Go down in the Tiel men's company and pay what the count's men ask: thirty pennies
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s06.out_company (a true price word: Rhine wine is dear at Lunden for ninety days, because of this toll)

options.label: Take the back creeks on the night tide
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s06.out_creeks_success or .out_creeks_failure (the skipper warns first; caught, she pays the toll and half again)

options.label: Hear the Tiel men out, and cut their count of it on your stick
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s06.out_hear (costs nothing)

memory.company: sailed in the Tiel men's company

cards.note: Step 7, a turn (drawn at Ahus, Hleidr, Sliesthorp or Ripa in 1026, once the story has begun). The king's fleet after the Holy River. Sources: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle E under 1025: the king went to Denmark with ships to the holm at the Holy River, Ulf and Eglaf came against him with a great force by land and sea from Sweden, very many were lost on the king's side, Danish and English, and the Swedes held the field (our rendering; dossiers/ahus.md quotes Ingram 1823); the battle is put in 1025 or 1026 and the sources disagree on who won (?); the game's card uses 1026. Godric, the wounded shipman, is invented. Sets ch_cnut_1016_7; _fed_fleet, _carried_wounded (the reckoning of 1035 reads it).
cards.when: moored and (port.id = ahus or port.id = hleidr or port.id = sliesthorp or port.id = ripa) and year = 1026 and flag.ch_cnut_1016_2 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_7

kings_man.note: a steersman of the king's fleet, buying stores; invented, unnamed

survivor.note: Godric, a shipman of Lunden in the king's pay, a spear through the thigh; invented

cards.title: After the Holy River
cards.intention: This year the king went with his ships to the Holy River, and Ulf and Eglaf came against him out of Sweden by land and by sea. Very many were lost on the king's side, Danes and English both. The fleet is buying bread, and the wounded lie in the boat sheds.

options.label: Sell the fleet your bread, meat and drink at the king's price
options.check: hold.ale > 0 or hold.ships_bread > 0 or hold.salt_pork > 0 or hold.herring > 0 or hold.cheese > 0
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s07.out_sell (the turn: 90 d over the market from the king's man, and stores dear here for thirty days)

options.label: Take Godric and three more home to the Thames, for nothing
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s07.out_wounded (costs four places in the boat; the shipmen of Lunden remember it in 1035)

options.label: Keep clear of a beaten fleet, and listen
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s07.out_clear (costs nothing; the news goes home with her)

memory.sell: sold stores to the king's fleet

cards.note: Step 8, the choice of roads (drawn at Lundenwic, Hamwic, Sarre, Hleidr, Ripa or Sliesthorp from June 1026 to February 1027, once the story has begun). A priest of the king's household writes down what was taken from the king's people on the roads. Sources: the letter of 1027 says the king spoke with the emperor, the pope and the princes 'about the needs of all the people of my whole realm, English and Danes' (William of Malmesbury, Gesta regum II.183; John of Worcester under 1031; our rendering): that he came with their complaints is in the letter, that a priest gathered them from shipmen is ours (?). The king kept Christmas 1026 in Denmark (later_ports/scandinavia.md: Ulf killed at Roskilde) and went to Rome from there. The emperor's men at Lunden and their Christmas and Easter dues: IV Aethelred 2 (lore/law_tolls.md 7.4). The Cologne man is invented, unnamed. Sets ch_cnut_1016_8 and one road: _witness (with _named, the cost that lasts), _plain or _sold.
cards.when: moored and (port.id = lundenwic or port.id = hamwic or port.id = sarre or port.id = hleidr or port.id = ripa or port.id = sliesthorp) and ((year = 1026 and month >= 6) or (year = 1027 and month <= 2)) and flag.ch_cnut_1016_2 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_8

clerk.note: a priest of the king's household with wax tablets; invented, unnamed

merchant.note: a wine merchant of Cologne, one of the emperor's men; invented, unnamed

cards.title: What was taken, and by whom
cards.intention: The king means to be at Rome when the emperor is crowned, and he will not go with an empty mouth. A priest of his household sits in the church porch with wax tablets and asks every shipman what was taken from him on the roads, and by whom.

options.label: Lay your tally sticks on his table and say all of it, before witnesses
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s08.out_witness (the honest road, to the ending rhine_named; the cost that lasts: her name is on the tablets, and the toll men of the Rhine will hear it)

options.label: Tell him what the pilgrims say of the barriers in the mountains
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s08.out_plain (costs nothing; to the ending kings_peace, which is what happened)

options.label: Take the Cologne man's two hundred pennies and leave the Rhine off the tablets
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s08.out_sold (the turn: 200 d; to the ending emperors_man)

memory.sold: sold a tally to the Cologne men

cards.note: Step 9 (at sea, May to October 1027, after step 8; not needed for an ending). The news from Rome reaches a ship before it reaches a town. Sources: the emperor Conrad crowned at Rome on Easter day, 26 March 1027, with Cnut and King Rudolf of Burgundy present (Wipo, Gesta Chuonradi 16); the letter sent home to England, by the hand of Lyfing, abbot of Tavistock (John of Worcester under 1031) (?); pilgrims home from Rome carry palms (the 'palmer' of later speech; the custom this early (?)). The meeting is ours. Sets ch_cnut_1016_9; _early_word.
cards.when: under_way and year = 1027 and month >= 5 and month <= 10 and flag.ch_cnut_1016_8 and not flag.ch_cnut_1016_9

skipper.note: a Frisian skipper out of the Rhine mouth; invented, unnamed

pilgrim.note: Toke of Jutland, if his toll was paid at Cologne; else a pilgrim like him

cards.title: Palms on their staffs
cards.intention: A Frisian keel out of the Rhine mouth, deep with people. They have dry palm leaves tied to their staffs, and one of them is shouting across the water about the king.

options.label: Take three of them aboard for the Thames: they have walked far enough
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s09.out_aboard (the whole story on the way home, and a true price word: English cloth goes up the Rhine in numbers next spring)

options.label: Lie alongside: the Dane from the toll bank at Cologne knows your boat
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s09.out_gift (a pound of pepper bought at Pavia for the forty-five pennies, and the same price word)

options.label: Wave, and hold your course
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s09.out_wave (costs nothing; she hears it later with everyone else)

cards.note: Ending 1, what happened (drawn at an English port from July 1027 to 1034, on the plain road, or if step 8 never came). The king's letter is read to the English. Sources: the letter of 1027 in William of Malmesbury, Gesta regum II.183, and John of Worcester under 1031 (our rendering; lore/law_tolls.md section 10; chronicle_793.json 1027-03-26-cnut-rome): the emperor and King Rudolf, 'who holds most of those barriers', grant that the king's people, 'merchants as well as those who travel to pray', go to Rome and come home in firm peace and just law, free of barriers and toll-takers; the king bids his reeves do no man wrong, and wants plough-alms, tithes, Rome-penny and church-scot paid before he lands. Lyfing, abbot of Tavistock, carried it and was made bishop of Crediton in 1027 (?). That it was read in the ports, and that a reeve gave a merchant the king's writ of protection after it, are ours (?); the writ is the spine's en_cnut_peace. Sets ch_cnut_1016_end_kings_peace; grand rewards unlock_title_kings_protection, unlock_plot_lundenwic, unlock_factor_lundenwic.

abbot.note: Lyfing, abbot of Tavistock, bishop of Crediton from 1027; historical

reeve.note: the king's reeve of the port; invented, unnamed

cards.title: The king's letter
cards.intention: This year Abbot Lyfing came home from Rome with the king's letter, and it was read to the English in their own tongue. The king has spoken with the emperor and with King Rudolf, who holds the barriers in the mountains. His people, merchants as well as those who go to pray, shall go to Rome and come home in peace, free of the barriers and the toll-takers.

options.label: Ask for the king's writ of protection for your house and keel
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_kings_peace.out_writ (finale: 600 d and the king's protection; the reckoning of 1035 asks whose writ it is then)

options.label: Take the writ, and a reeve's man to keep your goods: you paid for others on the road
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_kings_peace.out_both (the kinder road: 900 d and two grand rewards, for the wounded carried or the pilgrims' toll paid)

options.label: Ask for ground at the hythe, held under the king's peace
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_kings_peace.out_plot (finale: 650 d and a plot at Lunden; ground does not lapse with a king)

options.label: Ask for nothing written: take the road's first fruits, and a man at the hythe
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_kings_peace.out_goods (finale: 250 d, six pounds of pepper and a bolt of silk, about 900 d, and a factor at Lunden; nothing for a later king to unmake)

memory.both: took the writ and a factor

cards.note: Ending 2, history changed (drawn at an English port from July 1027 to 1034, on the witness road). The letter as it is read names the river road as well as the mountain road. WHAT IS TRUE: the letter of 1027 names the road to Rome, the barriers and King Rudolf (William of Malmesbury, Gesta regum II.183); it does not name the Rhine, Cologne or the count's water, and the men of Cologne have no known freedom from the English king, nor the English at Cologne, before the twelfth century (Henry II's protection for the Cologne men at London, about 1157 (?)). WHAT IS CHANGED: the king has a shipman's tally and asks the emperor for the river too. Sets ch_cnut_1016_end_rhine_named and changed_cnut_letter_rhine; grand rewards unlock_charter_colonia, unlock_title_thegn (the merchant's thegn-right of Gethyncthu: 'thrice over the wide sea by his own means', story/unlocks_793.json), unlock_title_kings_protection, unlock_plot_lundenwic; the cost that lasts is ch_cnut_1016_named, set in step 8.

reeve.note: the king's reeve of the port; invented, unnamed

cards.title: The river in the letter
cards.intention: This year Abbot Lyfing came home from Rome with the king's letter, and it was read to the English in their own tongue. It speaks of the barriers in the mountains, as everyone knew it would. Then it speaks of the river road: of the bank at Cologne and the water below Tiel. The abbot looks up from the leaf to see who is listening.

options.label: Take the emperor's grant: your keel free of toll at Cologne
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_rhine_named.out_charter (finale: 900 d and the charter at Cologne)

options.label: Take the grant and the king's word that you are worthy of a thegn's right
options.check: flag.ch_cnut_1016_tally_rhine and flag.ch_cnut_1016_tally_merwede and (flag.ch_cnut_1016_carried or flag.ch_cnut_1016_carried_wounded or flag.ch_cnut_1016_paid_pilgrims)
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_rhine_named.out_thegn (the hard road: 1,800 d and two grand rewards, for both tallies and a service done on the way)

options.label: Take the king's writ of protection, good on the count's water
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_rhine_named.out_water (finale: 800 d and the king's protection)

options.label: Ask for nothing with a seal on it: take silver, and ground at the hythe
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_rhine_named.out_ground (finale: 1,100 d and a plot at Lunden)

memory.thegn: was named worthy of a thegn's right

cards.note: Ending 3, the tally sold (drawn at Lundenwic or Colonia from July 1027 to 1034, on the sold road). The letter says nothing of the Rhine, as in truth it did not, and the Cologne men keep a place for the one who kept it so. Sources: the emperor's men at Lunden, 'worthy of good laws, as we are', and their dues at Christmas and Easter of two grey cloths and one brown, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two kegs of vinegar (IV Aethelred 2, in the Latin of the Quadripartitus; lore/law_tolls.md 7.4; the date argued, about 1000 or under Cnut (?)); story/unlocks_793.json unlock_title_emperors_man. That they took in a stranger for a service is ours (?). Sets ch_cnut_1016_end_emperors_man; grand rewards unlock_title_emperors_man, unlock_factor_colonia, unlock_pilot_rhine; the cost that lasts is ch_cnut_1016_sold_tally.

pilgrim.note: an English widow back from Rome by the Rhine; invented, unnamed

cards.title: A place at the Cologne board
cards.intention: The king's letter has been read. It speaks of the mountains and of King Rudolf's barriers, and it does not speak of the Rhine. The men of Cologne trade as before, and at Christmas they bring the reeve his pepper, his gloves and his vinegar. They have kept a place for you at their board.

options.label: Sit down among the emperor's men, and trade as one of them
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.end_emperors_man.out_seat (finale: 600 d and the emperor's men's law at Lunden)

options.label: Ask for a man of theirs at Cologne to keep your goods

cards.note: Step 13, the reckoning (drawn at an English or Danish port from November 1035 to 1037, after any ending). Sources: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 1035-1036 (C, D and E), our rendering: Cnut died at Shaftesbury on 12 November (the morrow of Martinmas) and was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester; at Oxford Earl Leofric, almost all the thegns north of the Thames and the shipmen (lithsmen) of Lunden chose Harold to hold England, Earl Godwine and the men of Wessex withstood it, and the queen sat at Winchester with the king's housecarls; Harthacnut stayed in Denmark; Gunhild, Cnut's daughter, married King Henry, the emperor's son, at Nijmegen in 1036 (Wipo 35 (?)). That a dead king's writ must be bought again from the next is the custom of the charters. Sets ch_cnut_1016_13; _confirmed, or ch_cnut_1016_writ_void (the integrator should then withdraw unlock_title_kings_protection and en_cnut_peace if this chain alone gave them). The text 'deor' is in texts_793.json.

cards.title: One man's peace
cards.intention: This year King Cnut died at Shaftesbury, on the morrow of Martinmas, and they carried him to Winchester. The shipmen of Lunden and the thegns north of the Thames have chosen Harold. The queen sits at Winchester with the housecarls. Harthacnut is in Denmark and does not come.

options.label: Buy the new lord's word over the old king's writing: a hundred and twenty pennies
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s13.out_confirm (the writ stands under Harold, or under Harthacnut's men in Denmark)

options.label: Let the shipmen of Lunden speak for you: they remember who carried their wounded home
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s13.out_shipmen (the writ stands, for nothing: the men who chose the king vouch for her)

options.label: You hold of the emperor, not of a dead king: buy cloth while the English quarrel
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s13.out_board (a true price word: cloth cheap at Lunden while nobody knows whose reeve takes the toll, and dear at Cologne)

options.label: Let the old writing lie in the chest: it was one man's peace
options.note: outcome: chain_cnut_1016.s13.out_lapse (costs the writ, if there was one, and nothing else; a poem for the chest)
